headline: Iran blockade revival sends oil up ~9%, chips and growth stocks drag S&P 500 and Nasdaq lower into a week stuffed with CPI, bank earnings, and Fed Chair Warsh's first congressional testimony.
stance: The macro table is set for a binary day: a headline CPI print that consensus expects to go negative month-on-month (-0.1%) lands at 8:30 ET, followed by JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and Bank of America earnings. The headline number will likely look disinflationary — do not be fooled. Core CPI is expected to hold near 2.9% year-on-year, still running well above the Fed's 2% target; the energy relief that drives the soft headline reflected June gasoline prices that have already partially reversed with the Strait of Hormuz re-closure. Futures are modestly softer overnight (S&P –0.2%, Nasdaq –0.3%), consistent with wait-and-see positioning ahead of the data.

news.head: Trump reinstates Iran blockade
news.body: President Trump announced he is reinstating what he called a blockade on Iranian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, sparking a roughly 9% single-day surge in WTI crude to ~$78/bbl and Brent to ~$83/bbl on Monday.

news.head: CPI June due 8:30 ET today
news.body: Consensus expects headline CPI to fall 0.1% month-on-month — which would trim the annual rate from 4.2% to ~3.9% — but core CPI is forecast to stay sticky near 2.9% year-on-year, keeping the Fed in a difficult spot.

news.head: Big-bank earnings kick off
news.body: JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, and Bank of America are among the first major banks to report Q2 results today, marking the unofficial start of an earnings season where S&P 500 companies are expected to post roughly 24% profit growth.

news.head: TSMC June revenue surges 68% YoY
news.body: Taiwan Semiconductor reported June 2026 consolidated revenue of approximately NT$442.68 billion, up 67.9% year-on-year and 6.2% from May, with H1 revenue up 35.6%; Q2 full earnings call is scheduled for July 16.

news.head: Fed Chair Warsh testifies to Congress
news.body: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first semi-annual monetary policy testimony to Congress today (Tuesday), with markets watching for any signal on whether a September rate hike remains on the table — currently priced at a meaningful probability.

news.head: SK Hynix Seoul reversal drags Asia
news.body: SK Hynix shares tumbled more than 15% in Seoul on Monday as investors booked profits following its record Nasdaq IPO debut, dragging South Korea's Kospi down nearly 9% and Japan's Nikkei 225 down ~1.9%.

news.head: China June exports beat
news.body: China's June exports came in above expectations, providing some macro support even as domestic demand remains subdued — a mild positive for global cyclical sentiment.

implications: Oil at $78/bbl (WTI, prior cash close) with the Strait of Hormuz dispute live again means the June CPI 'relief' on energy is already backward-looking; real-time reflationary pressure is rebuilding.

Core CPI's expected 2.9% print is the number the Fed actually targets — if it surprises to the upside, expect the 10-year yield (prior close 4.62%) to push higher and growth stocks to sell off further.

A soft headline CPI could temporarily lift risk assets in the first 30 minutes after the 8:30 print; watch whether the rally holds into the bank earnings — a failure to hold would be a bearish signal for the session.

Bank earnings (JPM, GS, BAC today; MS, BNY, BlackRock Wednesday) arrive with credit spreads still historically contained — HY-IG spread 269 bps, IG OAS 77 bps — providing a constructive backdrop for financial sector results.

Positioning: In rates, speculators have almost no bullish bets left on 3-month SOFR futures (2nd percentile of three years) — a contrarian floor for bonds if CPI surprises softer. In equities, Russell 2000 futures show the same pattern — specs at the 2nd percentile, a contrarian-bullish lean for small-caps. In FX, British Pound specs are at the 2nd percentile (extended short positioning, contrarian-bullish). In commodities, Copper specs are at the 94th percentile — speculators are heavily positioned long copper, a contrarian warning as WTI specs are also near lows (10th percentile, contrarian-bullish for oil).

watch.head: 8:30 ET — June CPI
watch.body: The single most important number of the day: consensus headline -0.1% MoM / ~3.9% YoY, core +0.2-0.3% MoM / ~2.9% YoY — any upside surprise on core would likely push yields higher and pressure the S&P 500.

watch.head: Pre-open — JPM, GS, BAC earnings
watch.body: The big banks report before the open; net interest income guidance and credit loss commentary will be the key market movers, not just the headline EPS beats.

watch.head: ~TBD — Fed Chair Warsh testimony
watch.body: First congressional appearance as Fed chair; any language tightening the door on cuts — or opening it — will move both bond yields and the dollar materially.

watch.head: 9:15 ET — Industrial Production / Capacity Utilization (June)
watch.body: A secondary macro read on real economic momentum, coming alongside the inflation print.

watch.head: 10:00 ET — Michigan Consumer Sentiment (July prelim)
watch.body: Watch the one-year inflation expectations sub-index: it climbed to 3.7% in June — any further rise would add hawkish pressure on the Fed.

watch.head: Crude oil intraday
watch.body: WTI closed ~$78/bbl (prior cash close) after a near-9% surge Monday; any fresh Hormuz headline could push energy stocks sharply in either direction through the session.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.62% (prior cash close Jul 13) — up materially from 4.56% a week ago as oil-driven inflation fears reignited.
2-year yield at 4.26% (prior cash close Jul 13), giving a 2s-10s curve of +36 bps — positively sloped but narrow, signaling the market does not fully trust the growth outlook.

10-year breakeven inflation (the bond market's price-inflation gauge) sits at 2.26% (prior close Jul 13) — relatively contained versus 4.2% actual headline CPI in May, suggesting bond buyers are betting energy shock is temporary.
Real (inflation-adjusted) 10-year rate is 2.36% (prior close Jul 13) — high by recent history and a meaningful headwind for expensive growth stocks.

The MOVE index — a measure of bond-market volatility, the rates equivalent of the VIX — sits at 77.8 (prior close Jul 13), relatively calm given the geopolitical backdrop, which may mean today's CPI is a bigger volatility event than current pricing implies.
Markets price a ~68% chance the Fed holds rates unchanged at the July meeting; a September hike remains in play, especially if today's core CPI does not soften.

The Fed's reverse repo facility — a key daily gauge of excess cash sloshing through the banking system — has nearly drained to $0.8bn (Jul 13), meaning the plumbing of markets is running lean; any sudden liquidity need would show up quickly in funding costs.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left on 3-month SOFR (short-term interest rate) futures — sitting at the 2nd percentile of their 3-year range — a contrarian floor for bonds. Specs and commercial hedgers sit at opposite extremes, historically a reliable mean-reversion signal.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: S&P 500 prior cash close: 7,515.34 (down 0.79% on Mon Jul 13); overnight S&P 500 futures pointing roughly -0.2% as of pre-market ~6am ET.
Nasdaq Composite prior cash close: 25,873.18 (down 1.55% Mon), with Nasdaq-100 futures off ~-0.3% overnight — tech bore the brunt of the oil-inflation-rate anxiety.
Dow Jones Industrial Average prior cash close: 52,498.64 (down 0.26%, or 138 points Mon).
VIX (the S&P 500 fear gauge) closed at 17.16 (prior close Jul 13) — elevated but not panicked; VXN (Nasdaq equivalent) at 27.3, reflecting more stress in tech.

SKEW index at 145.7 (prior close Jul 13) — elevated, meaning the options market is pricing a meaningfully higher probability of a large downside move than a normal distribution would suggest; tail-risk hedging is live.
Breadth is holding: 65.8% of S&P 500 names trade above their 50-day average and 68.1% above their 200-day average (as of Jul 10) — the selloff is concentrated in large-cap tech, not broad.

The equity risk premium — roughly, the extra return stocks offer versus safe bonds — is at -2.05% (Jun 30 reading), meaning stocks as a group offer essentially zero extra compensation over risk-free Treasuries at current price levels; this is a valuation warning at a CAPE of 41.85.
TSMC reported June revenue up 67.9% year-on-year; Q2 earnings call is July 16 — this is the AI supply-chain litmus test for the entire semiconductor sector.
Bank earnings week begins today with JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and Bank of America; Q2 S&P 500 EPS growth expectations are running near 24% year-on-year — a high bar.
sections.positioning: Russell 2000 (small-cap) futures specs are at the 2nd percentile of their 3-year positioning range — speculators have almost no bullish bets left, a contrarian-bullish lean for small-caps relative to large-cap tech.

single_name.note: Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) — the world's dominant AI chip foundry — just posted June revenue +67.9% year-on-year; with large off-exchange block buying (quiet institutional accumulation) and a burst of unusual options buying flagged in our scan, and company insiders have been buying, this is a fresh long setup above its 200-day line ahead of Q2 earnings on July 16.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: High-yield to investment-grade bond spread at 269 bps (as of Jul 10) — credit markets remain relatively calm, not pricing a recession or a funding crisis despite the geopolitical noise.

Investment-grade option-adjusted spread at 77 bps (Jul 10) — tight by historical standards, meaning corporate borrowers of high quality are not paying a significant risk premium; supportive of equities.
Commercial paper funding rate (CPFF spread) at 18 bps (Jul 10) — short-term corporate borrowing markets are functioning normally; no stress signal.
Bank credit growth running at 5.93% year-on-year (Jul 1) — solid but not frothy, consistent with an economy that is growing but slowing.
M2 money supply growing 5.58% year-on-year (May) while the Fed balance sheet is expanding only 1.11% year-on-year (Jul 8) — the money supply is being driven by bank lending, not Fed printing.
4-week average jobless claims of 219K (week ending Jul 4) remain low, consistent with a still-tight labor market and limited near-term recession signal.
Financial conditions indexes (ANFCI -0.51 z-score, STLFSI -0.72) remain loose — meaning the broader lending and credit environment is still easy, which supports risk assets even as rates rise.

single_name.note: Scorpio Tankers (STNG) — product tanker operator — sits at the intersection of energy and credit themes: with the Strait of Hormuz dispute live, tanker day-rates could spike; large off-exchange block buying (quiet institutional accumulation), a burst of unusual options buying, and two insider buying signals have fired, with the stock trading above its 200-day line. Shorts hold 2.2 days-to-cover — a moderate squeeze risk if tanker rates move.
